_README: utilities.json — which utility serves a point, and whether it publishes a
hosting-capacity map this tool can read.
WHY THIS FILE EXISTS
The territory boundary used to be four numbers inline in the probe. Going
national means the question 'whose wire is this' has to be answered before
'how much room is on it', and the answer is different in every state.
WHAT 'NATIONAL' ACTUALLY MEANS HERE
There is no national hosting-capacity dataset. Nobody publishes one. The
DOE keeps an ATLAS of the maps that exist, and as of its May 2024 edition
that was 58 utilities and state agencies across 26 states, DC and Puerto
Rico — and DOE is explicit that it does not maintain those maps, only the
list. https://www.energy.gov/cmei/us-atlas-electric-distribution-system-hosting-capacity-maps
So the honest ceiling for circuit-level answers is roughly half the states,
partial within them. Everywhere else the tool still works — address,
position, satellite, parcel, notes, starring, export — it simply has no
wire to read. That is what `hasMap: false` and `hasMap: null` mean below,
and why the card says 'no utility mapped' rather than 'circuit unknown'.
TWO SEPARATE PROBLEMS, DELIBERATELY KEPT APART
1. WHICH UTILITY serves a point. Solvable nationally today: HIFLD and
EIA publish Electric Retail Service Territories as polygons. The bbox
entries here are a coarse stand-in so the tool works before that layer
is wired; they OVERLAP and they are wrong at the edges, which is why
`bboxIsApproximate` is true on every one of them.
2. WHETHER THAT UTILITY PUBLISHES CAPACITY, and at what URL. Not solvable
centrally. One utility at a time, same as counties.json.
EVERY endpoint below is null except ComEd. That is deliberate and it is
not laziness: an endpoint guessed from a pattern is worse than no endpoint,
because it fails as 'no capacity here' rather than as 'not configured', and
a rep reads that as a dead site. Run verify_utilities.py to discover and
confirm one, exactly as verify_counties.py does for assessors.
`verified: true` means: an endpoint was called, it returned features, and
the field names were read off the response. Nothing else earns it.

_source.territories: HIFLD / EIA-861 Electric Retail Service Territories (not yet wired)
_source.note: The atlas is the worklist. Work down it; do not guess endpoints.

utilities.name: ComEd
utilities.note: The only one confirmed against live data. Service name carries a month (JUN2026) and rotates quarterly — the Worker's UPSTREAM constant has to follow it, and when it does not, every layer returns 403.

utilities.name: Ameren Illinois
utilities.note: Downstate Illinois, adjacent to ComEd. Same state, same regulator, so the most likely second utility. Check the DOE atlas entry for Illinois.

utilities.name: Joint Utilities of New York
utilities.legalName: ConEd, National Grid, NYSEG, RG&E, Central Hudson, Orange & Rockland
utilities.note: Six utilities publishing to a COMMON methodology under a PSC roadmap, which is unusual and valuable — one adapter may serve all six. Storage-specific fields were added and the maps were enhanced in April 2026, including scheduled-operation storage fields. https://jointutilitiesofny.org/utility-specific-pages/hosting-capacity

utilities.name: PG&E
utilities.note: California's three IOUs publish Integration Capacity Analysis maps under CPUC order. ICA is the same idea as hosting capacity with different vocabulary — expect the field names to differ substantially from ComEd's.

utilities.name: Southern California Edison
utilities.note: See pge-ca. Same CPUC ICA framework.

utilities.name: San Diego Gas & Electric
utilities.note: See pge-ca. Same CPUC ICA framework.

utilities.name: Xcel Energy (Minnesota)
utilities.note: Minnesota was an early hosting-capacity state. Xcel appears in the DOE atlas; confirm which of its operating companies the map covers.

utilities.name: Xcel Energy (Colorado)
utilities.note: Named in the DOE atlas coverage. Separate map from the Minnesota one despite the shared brand — treat as two utilities, not one.

utilities.name: Pepco Holdings
utilities.legalName: Potomac Electric Power Co, Delmarva, Atlantic City Electric
utilities.note: Exelon sibling of ComEd, which is the reason to try it early: an Exelon utility is more likely than most to publish on the same Esri platform with a similar schema, so the existing adapter may largely work.

utilities.name: Eversource
utilities.note: Massachusetts has a hosting-capacity requirement; confirm whether the map spans all three states or Massachusetts only.

utilities.name: National Grid (Massachusetts)
utilities.note: Distinct from the New York National Grid entry inside ju-ny. Same parent, different regulator, probably a different map.

utilities.name: DTE Energy
utilities.note: Michigan appears in the atlas; confirm DTE versus Consumers coverage.

utilities.name: Hawaiian Electric
utilities.note: Very high DER penetration, so hosting capacity is unusually binding — a market where this tool's core question matters more than most.

utilities.name: Texas (ERCOT area)
utilities.note: ⚠ THE BIGGEST STORAGE MARKET IN THE COUNTRY AND THE THINNEST DATA. Texas leads US battery build-out by a wide margin, but the deregulated market splits wires from retail across many TDUs (Oncor, CenterPoint, AEP Texas, TNMP) and Texas is not among the states with a public hosting-capacity mandate. Expect no map. Plan on interconnection queues and direct TDU contact instead — and do not let the absence read as 'no opportunity', because it is the opposite.
